title: Gandhi's Gita: the war inside
hookLine: a law student in London is handed his own family's book, in English
carry: karma yoga: the work is yours, not the fruit
tomorrow: how does a Baptist pastor end up with a Hindu's method?

lines: A FAMILY BOOK, IN SOMEONE ELSE'S LANGUAGE.
cards: Someone at a dinner party hands over a book your own family has kept for generations, in English, and asks what you make of it. You've never actually read it. That's where Gandhi is, as a young law student in London.

Two brothers he's met there are reading the Bhagavad Gita in an English translation, and they ask him to read it with them. He's ashamed: he has never read it in Sanskrit, or in Gujarati, his own language. So he opens it.
And the book begins with two armies lined up for war, and a god telling a frightened prince to stand up and fight.

teach.b: So how does the man who wouldn't strike back end up calling this book his guide? In his autobiography, Gandhi says the Gita became his guide for daily conduct, a book he reached for again and again.
His answer was a way of reading.

teach.h: KARMA YOGA: DO THE WORK, LET GO OF THE FRUIT.
teach.b: Later he translated the Gita into Gujarati with his own notes, and named it Anasakti Yoga, the yoga of non-attachment.
There he reads the battlefield of Kurukshetra as the human heart, where good and evil are always at war. Arjuna's real enemy is inside.
Then he leans on a line from the second chapter: your right is to the work, never to its fruits. Do the work fully; let go of the result. Hindus call this karma yoga, the path of action.
For Gandhi, that line was the engine of nonviolent struggle.
A satyagrahi could march, fast or go to jail without needing to see the win, because the work itself was the offering. Not every Hindu reads it his way.
Other readers take the battle as a real war and a real duty, and the Gita has room for more than one reader. But Gandhi's reading hands over something steady.

teach.h: THE FRUIT WAS NEVER YOURS TO HOLD.
teach.b: A setback isn't the end of the story, because the result was never the worker's to hold. The man of nonviolence found his steadiness in a war poem.

how: Gandhi's Gita commentary, Anasakti Yoga, is still read alongside the Gita itself, and its idea of acting without clinging to results is taught as karma yoga.

o: two rival leaders who argued over how to free India
two men joined by one idea: holding truth without harm
two friends who marched side by side in Alabama

games.q: what's inside Gandhi's Gita — tap the pairs.
p: the battlefield, read as the heart
marches without needing to see the win

s: letting go of the fruit means not caring about the work
the work is done fully; only the grip on the result is let go.
Gandhi first read the Gita in English, with two friends in London
he writes that he was ashamed he hadn't read it in Sanskrit or Gujarati.
every Hindu reads the Gita's battle as an inner war
Gandhi did; other readers take it as a real war and a real duty.

games.q: you spent weeks organizing a food drive at school, and hardly anyone came. by Gandhi's reading of the Gita, what now?
o: call it a failure: the turnout is how you know the work mattered.
do the work again, fully, and hold the turnout loosely.
wait until you can be sure the next one will be a big hit.
games.why: Gandhi leaned on Gita 2.47: your right is to the work, never to its fruits. a setback isn't the end, because the result was never yours to hold.

practice: If there's paper nearby, write down one task in front of you this week, the real one. Under it, leave a blank line where the result would go, and leave it blank.
If you pray, offer the task the way Krishna asks in the Gita: whatever you do, do it as an offering. If you don't, simply set it down as the work, done well.
Breathe with the page in front of you: the work is written, and the result stays open.

wordCard.voice: Gandhi and King: today, a war poem read as the war inside, and the work done without grabbing at its fruit.

orig.note: Sanskrit anasakti, non-attachment. Gandhi named his Gita Anasakti Yoga.

carryVoice: Something to keep from Gandhi's Gita: karma yoga. The work is yours, not the fruit. Until tomorrow.
